title: A platform for change? Core component innovations, complementor adaptation, and multihoming in platform‐based ecosystems
authors: Shiva Agarwal; Ram Ranganathan
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business Austin Texas USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Digital platforms coordinate complementor innovations through interfaces into their core components. However, when interfaces themselves evolve alongside core component innovations, complementors may exhibit behaviors that are not entirely predictable. Using granular data from Apple's five major iOS releases, we abductively examine App developers’ responses following Apple's core component innovations. We document that, in post‐release periods, complementors simultaneously increase co‐innovation on iOS while being more likely to multihome by diversifying to the competing platform. These choices are further explained by whether architectural changes reflect cross‐platform standardization or platform‐specific differentiation. Standardization spurs both complementor co‐innovation and multihoming, while differentiation reduces diversification tendencies. The patterns that we document reveal an important tension: governing through interfaces enables platforms’ scalability but constrains their ability to control complementors as platforms evolve. Managerial Summary Digital platforms like Apple coordinate large scale innovation through standardized interfaces, but those interfaces must evolve as platforms compete, and the direction of that evolution has consequences managers should attend to. Analyzing Apple's five major iOS releases, we find that architectural changes are associated with increased co‐innovation but also a higher likelihood that developers diversify to a competing platform. This pattern is particularly pronounced when updates bring iOS closer to Android, suggesting that architectural convergence may lower the barriers to cross‐platform expansion for developers. Importantly, this behavior is strongest among highest‐value developers. Platform managers should therefore treat architectural evolution not merely as a technical decision, but as a strategic one with direct implications for ecosystem loyalty, competitive differentiation, and the retention of valuable ecosystem partners.

title: Institutional Amnesia and the Loss of “The Why Rationale” in Central Government Agencies
authors: Alastair Stark; Hridesh Gajural; Jack Corbett; Dennis C. Grube; Heather Lovell; Rodney J. Scott
affiliations: School of Political Science and International Studies University of Queensland, St Lucia Campus Brisbane Australia; School of Regulation and Global Governance Australian National University Canberra Australia; School of Social Sciences Monash University Victoria Australia; Department of Politics and International Relations University of Cambridge Cambridge UK; University of Tasmania School of Geography, Planning, and Spatial Sciences, Sandy Bay Campus Tasmania Australia; School of Law RMIT Melbourne Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Data from 115 interviews conducted with officials in the Westminster systems of Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom is used to substantiate a corrosive relationship between institutional amnesia and the ability of public servants to make sense of their organizational context. A process in which public servants question why the policies, procedures, and organizational frameworks that surround them is proposed as one medium through which this relationship operates. Four problematic effects produced by this relationship and process are subsequently analyzed: (1) public servants following but not understanding procedures, (2) inexplicable organizational aspects getting abandoned, (3) the layering of new organizational features on top of old ones, creating complexity, and (4) public service inefficiencies and associated public servant frustration. The article concludes with the implications of this important relationship for public administration scholars and practitioners.

title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
authors: Holly Dykstra; Shibeal O’ Flaherty; Ashley Whillans
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Konstanz, 78464 Konstanz, Germany; and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), 75007 Paris, France; School for Government, King’s College London, London WC2R 2LS, United Kingdom; Negotiation, Organizations & Markets Unit, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163
abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
authors: Manish Raghavan
affiliations: Sloan School of Management and Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, MIT, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. title: Simulating competitive collocation strategies with deep reinforcement learning
authors: Roman Gwosdilin; Thomas Lindner; Michael Wolfesberger
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a simulation model based on deep reinforcement learning to study competitive collocation strategies of two internationalizing firms. Drawing on the strategic interaction and competitive collocation literature in IB, we explore the factors determining the performance-optimizing degree of collocation in market-seeking internationalization for a duopoly in product markets. Our simulation suggests that a high degree of collocation between the two firms is optimal in many circumstances. Whereas mid-to-high levels of collocation are driven by low competitive intensity, low entry barriers, low home-market size, and high market-size variation, complete collocation emerges under high competitive intensity, low first-mover advantage, and smaller home-market size. High entry barriers, combined with low variation in market size and strong liabilities of foreignness, drive the opposite case of complete mutual avoidance. A key takeaway from the simulation is a focus on the competing firm in global expansion: in many cases, it becomes key to limit the rival’s growth options and to enter key markets before access becomes more restricted. We discuss the possibilities of using computer-simulation-based approaches to theorizing on internationalization.

title: Routinized Deference: Predictive Screening and Bureaucratic Capacity in Child Protective Services
authors: Jiaen Wu
affiliations: Indiana University-Bloomington O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs, , 1315 East Tenth Street, Bloomington, IN 47405,
abstract: Abstract Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to support frontline decision-making in public administration, but evidence remains limited on how they affect bureaucratic capacity. This study examines county-level adoption of predictive screening tools in U.S. Child Protective Services using NCANDS data (2010–2023) and a stacked difference-in-differences design. Leveraging staggered adoption, I find no change in the total number of investigations opened and a sizable decline (about 15%) in the share of investigations that are substantiated. These results are inconsistent with operational capacity gains and more consistent with misclassification that erodes analytical capacity. These findings are consistent with a mechanism of routinized deference: under workload and accountability pressures, algorithmic recommendations can become procedurally defensible defaults. Overall, this study argues that predictive screening is not capacity-enhancing by default, as routinized deference can undermine the professional judgment central to bureaucratic work.

title: Regulatory Agencies Under Mutating Populism in Office: Insights From Italy (1990–2025)
authors: Fabrizio Di Mascio; Giulio Francisci; Martino Maggetti; Alessandro Natalini
affiliations: University of Turin Turin Italy; LUMSA University of Rome Rome Italy; University of Lausanne Lausanne Switzerland
abstract: ABSTRACT Our paper builds a bridge between the emerging strand of research on public administration under populist rule and the established literature on delegation to independent regulatory authorities (IRAs). We focus on Italy, a critical case in Western Europe, which between 2001 and 2025 experienced six coalition governments dominated or strongly influenced by populist parties of different ideological orientations. Findings highlight that delegation to IRAs is remarkably resilient once institutionalized, even under sustained political contestation. Despite repeated populist participation in government since the early 2000s, Italian IRAs have not been subject to systematic de‐delegation or statutory retrenchment. However, the preservation of formal independence has not implied the absence of means for political control. Our analysis shows that populist governments have systematically relied on political appointments. Interestingly, political appointments have not been driven by partisan loyalty or overt politicization. Instead, the intervention of populist parties has operated along a different dimension of political control that has received less attention in delegation theory: the specialization of appointees. Populist governments have displayed a preference for appointing IRAs' board members with lower levels of domain‐specific specialization, privileging generalist profiles over specialists.

title: Measuring Organizational Constructs in Large-Scale Text: An interpretive framework combining topic modeling and BERT
authors: Ana Alina Tudoran; Nicole Franziska Richter; Jeisson A. Higuera Reina; Surabhi Verma
abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
authors: Shumpei Iwao; Vatsal Mitesh Tailor; Qi Wu
abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

title: EXPRESS: Pricing and Information Provision in Service Platforms with Heterogeneous Customers
authors: Xin Weng; Lijian Lu; Li Xiao
abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers' decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

title: Multi-self presentation and knowledge contribution in platform operations: Evidence from a natural experiment
authors: Yingpeng Zhu; Zike Cao; Gen Li; Yi Yang; Liangfei Qiu
affiliations: University of Macau; Zhejiang University; Fudan University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Florida
abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users’ formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others’ questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature’s multi-self presentation function: first, the new feature increases high adopters’ engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users’ casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

title: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
authors: Daxuan Cheng; Lei Gao; Yin Liao; Zheyao Pan
abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive — the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

title: EXPRESS: From Institutional Expansion to Exposure-Driven Co-Evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
authors: Yinghao Pan; Dingyi Tang; Jie Wu; Yuan Sun; Liangfei Qiu
abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets Wu (2026a,b), which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement Wu’s analysis with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China’s growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China’s OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

title: Leading by example: how major customers shape suppliers' implementation of process-based rights
authors: Yinyin Cao; Yoon Hee Kim
affiliations: College of Business, University of Michigan-Dearborn Department of Management and Marketing, , , ,; Coles College of Business, Kennesaw State University , , ,
abstract: Purpose Drawing from research on dependence and embeddedness in supplier-major customer relationships, this study examines the implementation level of process-based rights (PBR) – including freedom of association, workforce diversity, and fair and non-discriminatory treatment of workers – within supplier-major customer dyads. The study also empirically investigates how customers' transactional governance and relationship history with suppliers interplay in suppliers' PBR implementation. Design/methodology/approach Using 482 unique supplier-major customer dyads over 14 years (2010–2024), we performed hierarchical analysis to estimate the direct and interaction effects of customers' PBR implementation, transactional governance, and relationship history on their suppliers' PBR implementation. Findings Our results show that major customers exert a significant influence on suppliers' PBR implementation. Furthermore, transactional governance and a long relationship history work in synergistic ways only when the customer itself demonstrates average to high levels of PBR, but not when customer PBR implementation levels are low. Originality/value As one of the first studies to explore PBR within supplier-major customer dyads, our findings underscore the important role of customers in leading the implementation of labor standards, rather than as an enforcer of labor standards, in motivating supplier compliance.

authors: Pepe Bellin; Norbert Homner; Erwin Fielt; Sebastian Gabriel; Martin Matzner
affiliations: Friedrich‐Alexander‐Universität Erlangen‐Nürnberg Nürnberg Germany; Audi AG Ingolstadt Germany; School of Information Systems Queensland University of Technology Brisbane Queensland Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Car manufacturers excel in leveraging new digital technologies through vehicle design but face challenges in using the data these technologies provide for innovation. In this practitioner paper, we analyse and report on the process AUDI, a German original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of premium automobiles, went through in developing and managing data‐driven business models. A detailed description of the three phases of the carmaker's journey from creating to scaling to capturing identifies the automotive industry's urgent need to standardise data, prioritise customer integration and overcome difficulties in determining the price of data. For other (European) car manufacturers developing and managing data‐driven business models, we also derive five lessons learned from our case regarding AUDI's efforts to address issues when leveraging car‐related data and present an industry outlook with remaining challenges.

title: Emerging Resistance in the Digital Transformation of Public Transport: Older Passengers With Dementia and Experiences of Ecobiographical Disruption
authors: James Rupert Fletcher
affiliations: Information, Decisions and Operations Division, School of Management University of Bath Bath UK
abstract: ABSTRACT The digital transformation of public transport is prone to resistance. Among the discontents of such transformation, older people and those living with cognitive impairments are repeatedly identified. Stereotypes assuming their innate resistance to technological change are widespread, but research shows that older people with dementia can have rich digital lives. This paper reports findings from an ethnography of public transport digital transformation with older passengers living with dementia in Greater Manchester, UK. Combining interviews, photography, poetry, route maps and contextual statistics, four cases illustrate the emergence of resistance to digital displays, cashless exchange, e‐ticketing and live routing. They reveal subtle, nuanced and contextually contingent resistances that emerge from digital transformation disrupting passenger ecobiographies—the rootedness of their lives in longstanding ecosystems. Findings show that everyday resistance can be small, transient and relational, and should be taken seriously as an indicator of potential injustices. Future initiatives should meaningfully include older and disabled users throughout to increase alertness to ecobiographical disruption and emerging resistance.

title:
<scp>CEO</scp>
                    Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of
                    <scp>CEO</scp>
                    Intentions Perspective
authors: Miao Yun; Longwang Fu
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

title: JACKKNIFE EMPIRICAL LIKELIHOOD FOR INFINITE-ORDER U -STATISTICS
authors: Qing Wang; Yichuan Zhao; Ting Zhang
affiliations: Wellesley College; Georgia State University; University of Georgia
abstract: Infinite-order U -statistics play a vital role in modern statistics. However, given their degree k n $k_n$ k Subscript n depends on the sample size n , quantifying their variability is quite challenging, as fixed-degree theories cannot be directly adopted. In this article, we propose a jackknife empirical likelihood (EL) framework that can be used to construct confidence intervals for an infinite-order U -statistic. We establish sufficient conditions for the limiting chi-squared distribution of the JEL ratio statistic and introduce an efficient partition-sampling realization for practical implementation. To evaluate the performance of the proposed methodology, we conduct simulation studies in the context of subsampling-based ensemble methods and the maximum test, respectively, comparing its performance with four competing methods. The simulation studies yield satisfactory results across the board. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of our method using a United States Forest Service timber auctions dataset to predict the highest bid at an auction.

Measuring Measurement Error
authors: N Aaron Pancost; Garrett Schaller
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin , McCombs School of Business; Colorado State University , College of Business
abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

title: Environmental Incidents and Sustainability Pricing Provisions
authors: HUYEN NGUYEN; SOCHIMA UZONWANNE
abstract: Abstract We investigate whether lenders use sustainability pricing provisions (SPPs) to manage borrower environmental risk. Using unexpected negative environmental incidents as shocks to environmental risk, we find that lenders are 10 percentage points less likely to include SPPs in loans to environmentally risky borrowers. Instead, they rely on conventional tools, including higher interest rates, stricter covenants, and collateral requirements. The effect weakens under strong institutional investor demand or when lenders can sell loans in secondary markets. Our study suggests that SPPs primarily help attract institutional investors rather than manage risk, with implications for the design and regulation of sustainability‐linked financial instruments.
